paras: The clubbing of a Black soldier by Chattanooga police took place on the evening of Monday, March 3, 1919, when Policeman J. H. Cornett struck one of a group of "Colored soldiers" on East Ninth street in Chattanooga, Tennessee. After a hearing at which many Black witnesses testified against the officers, Commissioner Betterton suspended Cornett and Patrolman Green and then discharged Cornett, who appealed to the full board. The Cleveland Advocate carried the case as news that a policeman had been dismissed for using force on a Black soldier.

According to a Chattanooga dispatch dated March 18, the trouble began over "a blockade of the sidewalk" by a number of Black soldiers on East Ninth street. Patrolman Green tried to disperse them, and the dispatch said there was "an indication that Officer Green would be overpowered," an explanation that matched the officers' side of the case. Cornett came to Green's aid with his club, and one soldier "suffered to some extent from licks by Cornett's club and some blood flowed." The soldier was not named, and the coverage does not say whether anyone was arrested.

Commissioner Betterton held a hearing in his office on the Friday before the dispatch. There, "a large number of Colored men testified against the officers," while the officers brought witnesses of their own in support of their account. Both officers were suspended as a result, and Cornett was afterward discharged for his "use of force." Cornett appealed the discharge to the full board, and no report of the board's decision was found.

The only report found is a short item on the front page of the Cleveland Advocate of March 22, 1919, printed among other race news briefs under the heading "Here is Example." The Advocate added no comment, but its account dwelt on the hearing, the Black testimony against the officers, and the policeman's dismissal rather than on the disturbance itself. Its explanation of the clubbing, the sidewalk blockade and the danger to Green, was given without attribution, although it matched the contention the officers put forward at the hearing.

reader.title: Clubbing of a Black soldier by Chattanooga police (1919)
bases: A Chattanooga policeman clubbed a Colored soldier while helping another patrolman disperse soldiers from a sidewalk, and was discharged for the use of force (A1).
Only one Black-press item, the Cleveland Advocate's Chattanooga dispatch, reports the incident (A1).

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Chattanooga dispatch)
accounts.gist: Cornett used force in helping Green quell a disturbance by Colored soldiers who blocked the sidewalk; one soldier was struck and bled, and the commissioner discharged Cornett after a hearing.

accounts.label: Officers' contention
accounts.gist: The officers brought witnesses in support of their version; the dispatch's explanation, a sidewalk blockade and a sign that Green would be overpowered, matches their side, though it is not attributed.

accounts.label: Colored witnesses at the hearing
accounts.gist: A large number of Colored men testified against the officers; their testimony is not described.

framing.detail: The Cleveland Advocate ran the dispatch without comment under 'Here is Example', stressing the officer's discharge for use of force.

info: One unnamed Colored soldier, among 'a number of Colored soldiers' involved, was struck with a policeman's club
Soldiers said to have blockaded the sidewalk; force explained by 'an indication that Officer Green would be overpowered' when he tried to disperse them
Policeman J. H. Cornett, who used his club while assisting Patrolman Green

sources.note: Chattanooga dispatch of March 18: Policeman J. H. Cornett discharged for clubbing a Colored soldier on East Ninth street March 3; appeal to full board.
quotes: One of the Colored soldiers suffered to some extent from licks by Cornett's club and some blood flowed.
It all came about by reason of a blockade of the sidewalk and an indication that Officer Green would be overpowered when he undertook to disperse the soldiers.
a large number of Colored men testified against the officers, while the latter introduced a number in support of their contention as to how it all happened.
